claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys have coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Rapid quenching from the melt captures a fine lamellar structure.
Rapid quenching followed by sub-eutectic annealing refines dual-phase lamellar-colony spacing.
Rapid quenching followed by sub-eutectic annealing strengthens interfacial cohesion between the two phases.
Sub-eutectic annealing relieves residual stresses introduced by rapid quenching.
Sub-eutectic annealing improves bonding at the internal phase interfaces.
Finer lamellae, residual-stress relief, and improved interfacial bonding reduce microcrack initiation at internal boundaries.
Reduced microcrack initiation permits more homogeneous tensile deformation.
Rapid quenching followed by sub-eutectic annealing will increase room-temperature yield strength relative to the conventional lamellar-colony baseline.
Rapid quenching followed by sub-eutectic annealing will increase room-temperature fracture or ultimate tensile strength relative to the conventional lamellar-colony baseline.
Rapid quenching followed by sub-eutectic annealing will retain or improve room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the conventional lamellar-colony baseline.
Conventionally processed as-cast or standard-annealed eutectic high-entropy alloys have high strength at the expense of limited ductility.
The treatment is effective only for compositions that support a eutectic microstructure.
The annealing temperature must be maintained just below the eutectic point for the treatment to be effective.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration can negate the benefit by coarsening the microstructure.
Insufficient cooling rate or annealing time can negate the benefit by failing to establish fine lamellae or adequate interfacial bonding.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis predicts improved ductility, whereas the predicted-outcome field allows mere retention of ductility.

The experiment requests identical casting conditions even though rapid quenching from the melt, rather than conventional processing, is the key intervention and necessarily changes the melt-solidification or casting cooling condition.
